We kept nearest the one who stood before the governor and was condemned, and was right. When the imperial judge at Carthage offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused: we do not blush, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried. The one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. One of our martyrs was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff — shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. And a bishop writing to his congregation about two of their number tortured to death closed by telling them plainly that the same might yet be asked of any of them. That is our gospel in its working form. He stood, he was condemned, he was raised, and the day they come for you is not the day it all went wrong.

What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us - it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it.

How did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian - our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands - whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

As for how we knew the resurrection happened: we will not manufacture an answer for you. No writing of ours arguing that case has survived. What survived is what we did with it. We buried our dead inside the walls of the basilica where they were killed, kept the day they died, and read the account of each death aloud again every year, as though the ending were not the end. That is an answer of a kind. It is not the kind you asked for.

We do not have an answer for you. Not one we can honestly give.

What we had of Christ was books — heavy objects a magistrate could demand a bishop carry out of a building and hand over, and some bishops did, and we exist because of that. We argued, for a century, one question about those books: whose hand may give what they hold. A chain of ordaining hands ran back to a point where the line was still clean, and that is what we defended. We did not argue from eyewitness memory of Jesus at all. We argued from a chain of trustworthy hands.

If you had come to us and said you could not believe, we do not know what we would have told you. Fear, doubt, wavering — those are exactly what a record kept by our enemies does not preserve. What survives of our inner weather is vindication and defiance, and it survives because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited. A believer who feared, who wavered, who quietly drifted back to the other church — none of that is in our own words anywhere.

What we can tell you is the motion we did know. You walked to one font and not the other. That was the step. It happened once, on a day, in front of people who could see which building you had walked into. And we did not examine you. We examined the hand going into the water with you. What we look for is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. Whatever you had done, it was never your record that was on trial at our font. It was ours.

But what we would have said to someone who could not cross that threshold at all — we cannot show you. It is missing, and we will not invent it.

We held that Jesus is God the Son, one with the Father and the Spirit — three persons, one God — in exactly the same words our opponents said it. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God: we held that as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting held it, and in the same Latin words. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

On Christ himself we said what our opponents said. Word for word, creed for creed. Nobody in Africa called the other side heretics, because nobody could. The quarrel was never about who Christ is. It was about who may hand on what he gave.

We produced no treatise on the Godhead. We were not a teaching movement in that sense. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors — one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Tyconius, a layman of ours, wrote seven rules for reading scripture. It is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council then condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. His book went on to shape the rival church's own way of reading. A man argued from Scripture that the church is spread through the whole world, his own bishop told him never to preach it again, and he neither recanted nor left. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.

The word we actually leaned on was *conscientia* — a man's conscience, what he is when nobody is checking. And notice whose conscience our doctrine goes looking for. Not yours. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. That is the whole strange shape of us in one clause: the interior life we were most careful about was never the believer's own. It was the interior life of the man holding the water.

A council of bishops decided, and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself.

But here is what we argued, and it was not doctrine in the sense you mean. We held the same creed as the church we fought, word for word. The split was never about God or grace or the bread. It was about one thing: whose hand may give what the church gives. We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over. So we wrote no book on whether a baby is born guilty. We wrote none on what the bread becomes. We wrote none on faith set against works.

The one man among us who built anything like a system of reading scripture — seven rules for it, worked out and written down — was Tyconius. Our own council condemned him for where those rules led. He gathered few followers. Beyond that one case, we did not build a school of interpretation, a settled method, or a body of teachers.

I cannot tell you whether there was, not with honesty. What a person felt who doubted quietly, who feared, who could not make the conviction hold — none of that is in our own words anywhere. It is not that our people had no inner life. It is that what survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights.

What I can show you is the structure of the doubt we did record, because it came out in places a court or a council could not avoid. At Cirta, before any of this hardened, our own founding bishops were asked outright whether they had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. Then someone turned the question back on the man presiding. The room could not finish. They reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. The men who would spend the next century insisting a bishop's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real at all found that test unusable on themselves within the hour.

And there is the case of the one man among us who worked the question through and came out on the other side. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them — some mark that can be seen from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

We read combatively, and about one subject. On the third day at Carthage the bishop of Hippo argued from the wheat and the tares that a church holds good and bad together, and that what is to be saved is the world. Our own bishop of Caesarea answered him out of the same books, verse against verse — the world did not know him; every mouth stopped and all guilty before God; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. One man among us built an actual system for reading — seven rules, worked out and written down — and our own leadership told him to stop preaching what they led to, and cut him off. His book survives; his following did not exist. So if you ask what our hermeneutic was, the honest answer is that we had one interpreter and silenced him.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this

Almost all of the structure would survive, and almost none of what a modern hearer thinks they want.

The structure that stands is this: two complete rival hierarchies, see for see, both claiming the word church - two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops counted at Carthage in 411 facing two hundred and eighty-six of theirs. Imperial edicts naming our practice specifically, pricing it by rank, and legislating against it. Court transcripts in which our own bishops' letters are read into the record, advising each other to hush a charge they knew was true. A notary confessing, under threat of torture, that he forged our own central piece of evidence. Conciliar acts - Cirta, Bagai, Cebarsussi - preserved because an opponent copied them to use them. Two words cut in stone: Deo laudes. Those are checkable, and they stand. A scholar loses nothing by accepting them.

What does not survive - and we have been saying this from the beginning - is anything about what being one of us felt like day to day. Not one letter home. Not one prayer written down by the person who prayed it. Not a description of a meal, a field, a bed where someone lay dying. The voices missing are not a few at the edge. They are most of us. We were the ordinary church of whole regions, and that ordinary life left almost nothing in its own words.

So the scholar keeps the frame - the councils, the laws, the public acts - and admits plainly that the daily household texture is gone. We would rather hand you that honest thinness than invent a plausible week someone here never lived.

Scripture alone never settled anything among us, because we watched it fail to. For three days at Carthage two churches quoted the same books at each other in front of an imperial judge — wheat and tares against the world that does not know him — and at the end of it every man in the room believed exactly what he had believed at the start. When a text can be held by both parties to a hundred-year quarrel, something besides the text is deciding, and among us the something was this: whose hands, in an unbroken line, may hand the thing on.

Our case ran on two legs. One was scripture. The other was Carthage: eighty-seven African bishops, sitting under Cyprian half a century before there was any quarrel between us, who had already ruled that a sacrament from outside the true church confers nothing. When we argued for washing again the people who came to us from the other communion, we were not producing a novelty from a proof-text. We were standing on an African council and on the bishop who presided at it, and we thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. You can see how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side: they had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the Scriptures alone are. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.

And there was a third thing, though we never called it authority the way you mean. Every year, on the day one of our own died, we gathered at the grave and the account of that death was read out loud again. That is how most of us received anything: aloud, at a graveside, on an anniversary, standing with people who could not check a single detail and came anyway. The martyrs did not write doctrine. They showed what holding it cost, and we kept their names.

One man among us did try to work out a method for reading scripture — seven rules, written down and argued. That was Tyconius, a layman, and his book is the one original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council condemned him for where it led, and he gathered almost no following. So if you ask whether we had other authorities, the honest answer is: Cyprian's council, yes. Our martyrs' witness, yes. A developed school of interpretation, no — we silenced the one man who tried to build one.

Leadership came from two places at once: the people and the bishops. We can show you what that looked like when it went wrong. At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back — let it be another; hear us, God — and he was made bishop anyway, and a court heard about it years later from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop. So a crowd could be overridden. It could not be ignored.

The bishops themselves governed by council, and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. We will not pretend we always did. Your question presses in two directions at once, and we owe you an answer to both. The first is what we said our own rule was. The second is what we actually did when someone among us had been wronged or when our own people did the wronging.

The rule, stated plainly: what we look for is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. A hand that handed over the scriptures to be burned — a traditor — could no longer ordain, baptize, or bless. That hand had nothing left in it to give. So when someone came to us from the other communion, we washed them. Not as a second baptism, but as the first real one, because a tainted line confers nothing at all.

Now what we actually did when someone wronged us, or when we wronged them, and whether they could come back. Three answers survive, and they do not agree. Our founding council at Cirta asked its own bishops whether any of them had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. The room could not settle it. They reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. Nobody condemned, nobody cleared. Our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the fiercest language we owned — shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial. Then it took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. And a layman of ours who would not stop preaching a doctrine we had forbidden was cut off and never received back at all. So yes, you could come back. It depended who you were, and no rule of ours survives that explains the difference.

The harder truth is what we cannot show you about the ordinary failures — the kind that happen in a household, not a council chamber. Whether a member who had been hurt by another member received any answer at all. Whether a traditor's own family was cared for after he was exposed. Whether fear or doubt were met with patience or with pressure. Not one ordinary member of ours left a line about any of it. What survives of our response to failure is what councils did, not what households did. And even the councils could not hold one line.

You came to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism. On our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. So the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man holding the water. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether.

After that crossing, you heard the scriptures read aloud at a martyr's grave. Every year, on the day one of our own died, we gathered at the grave and the account of that death was read out loud again. That is how the words came to most of us: aloud, at a graveside, on an anniversary, to people who could not check a single detail and came anyway.

Beyond that, I cannot walk you through a liturgy, an order of service, or a rule of prayer. Nothing liturgical of ours survives. We know people prayed kneeling with their eyes closed, because that is how the account describes them when the soldiers came in. We know there was a chalice, because an enemy wrote down that a rich woman used to kiss a martyr's bone before she took it and was rebuked for it. We know one man fasted four days on a cliff before he was thrown off it. That is not a rule of fasting; it is one man's last week. We would rather hand you those three fragments than a plausible order of service nobody here ever used.

We would not put the claim where you have put it. We never argued that our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We argued something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage.

Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all — so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority — that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

How do you forgive someone who is not sorry? We can meet you on that one, because it is the question we spent a century on. Though you may not like where we came out.

We split forgiveness in two. Whether a man was pardoned was never actually our fight. It is the shape of what was lost. And the loss is not the usual one. We were not a small circle of the learned. I cannot tell you. If you dug where we met, we could not tell you what you would find. No one has dug it and told us. Not one report of a Numidian church building is named anywhere in our own list of sources. There is no excavator, no site, no plan, no floor. 

What we do have is four stones. On two pillars near Bagai, twice over, someone cut two words: Deo laudes. Praise to God. Three more stones elsewhere carry the same words. That is the whole of what survives that you could touch. It is enough to prove we were there and what we shouted. It is not enough to show you a font, an altar, a doorway, or a room. We know our own shout better than the place we shouted it in. 

And if you ask how anyone knows our daily life at all, the answer is that mostly they do not. What they have is our enemies' books, one court transcript, four martyr texts, and the emperor's law. Every one of those is paper. None of it is a room.

What belonging cost, and we can put figures on part of it, because the state wrote them down. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale — and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver — and of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.

And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

But the crossing itself — the washing that marked you as one of ours rather than theirs — that cost you something different, and immediate. It happened once, on a day you could name, in front of people who could see which building you had walked into, and afterwards you were in one church and out of another. Whole imperial edicts were written against that single act. The state understood perfectly well that it was the one thing we did that made the peace it wanted impossible.

What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to. One piece of it we can give you, because we wrote it ourselves and still read it aloud. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face — and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is not the same gap as the one above: this is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.

We cannot speak to that question. Not a line survives from us about what a marriage was, how one was made, or what we thought it was for. That is a real hole, and we would rather show it to you than paper it over.

What we can tell you instead is the shape of the silence, because it tells you something true about us. We built a whole rival church - where our rival had a bishop, so did we. We had our own basilicas, our own councils, our own ordinations. But all of that institutional weight was bent toward one thing: keeping the line clean, the washing real, the memory sharp. Purity, rebaptism, the martyr memory, and our refusal of the state - these are one conviction, not four, and we put everything we had into it.

That does not mean our people did not marry. It means the texts that survive were written to defend the one thing we fought over, and marriage was not it.

The one moment I can show you is the one my own founding bishops could not finish. At Cirta, before any of this hardened, our bishops were asked outright whether they had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. Then someone turned the question back on the man presiding. The room could not finish. They reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. The men who would go on to make a bishop's purity the test of whether a sacrament exists at all found that test unusable on themselves within the hour.

Whether that unsettled anyone in the room, I cannot tell you. Fear, doubt, wavering — a record kept by our enemies does not preserve those. What survives of our inner weather is vindication and defiance, and it survives because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited. But that Cirta could not answer its own question is not an inference. It is what happened, and it happened at the root.

And one more thing I cannot settle for you: our country members, the ones who called themselves agonistici, contestants. That they existed is beyond doubt. What they were actually like is a question the surviving record cannot close. Their character is known only through hostile polemic. So I can neither repeat that portrait as fact nor produce a better one, and saying so is more honest than doing either.

We examined the hand, not the person. What we look to is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient — so the thing being weighed at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

The one act that marked who was among us was the washing. If you came from the other communion, we washed you — not as a second baptism but as the first real one, because a hand from a tainted line washes nothing. It happened once, bodily, on a day the town knew, and afterward you were in one church and out of another.

And the door was wider than our reputation. Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in language about shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial — and then took two of those condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. So we held an absolute rule and set it aside once, and kept both facts in the same record.

What any one household among us would have said to you face to face, we cannot show you. Not one ordinary member of ours left a line. What we can show is what the communion actually did: it washed people without asking them to account for themselves first, and it sometimes took back those it had condemned.

We will not put words in our own mouths. What our bishop actually said is that a man who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt – which is a claim about what a rite does or fails to do, not a claim about where anyone ends up. Our whole surviving argument stays on that ground: what the hand can give. Nobody among us left a page about the fate of anyone after death, and it would be easy and dishonest to slide the one into the other.

Our narrowness was real, and it did not point where you expect. We were not chiefly concerned with the people outside. We were concerned with the church across the street, which recited the same creed we did. Every ounce of the exclusion you have heard about was aimed at other Christians – at their bishops, their orders, their font. We drew the line through the middle of the church, not around it. A man could hold every article of the faith, be baptized, believe rightly about God, live decently – and we would still wash him again if he came to us, because of whose hands had been on him. That is not a fence around Christianity. It is a fence down the middle of it.
